subject: chemistry

moments.title: Whittingham's first Li battery
moments.body: Working at an oil company concerned about peak oil, Whittingham builds a lithium-titanium disulphide battery. The cells short and catch fire. Exxon abandons the project after the oil shock recedes.
moments.takeaway: The lithium-ion concept is born at an oil company, then dropped.

moments.title: Cobalt oxide cathode
moments.body: Goodenough finds that LiCoO2 is a stable, high-voltage cathode. The fundamental chemistry of modern Li-ion is fixed.
moments.takeaway: The cathode material that powers your phone is invented in Oxford.

moments.title: Graphite anode
moments.body: Yoshino combines LiCoO2 with a carbon (graphite) anode, eliminating metallic lithium and making cells safe enough to commercialise. Sony launches the first commercial Li-ion battery in 1991.
moments.takeaway: Combining the right cathode and anode produces a billion-unit-per-year technology.

moments.title: Nobel for Li-ion
moments.body: The three share the 2019 chemistry Nobel. Goodenough at 97 is the oldest ever Nobel laureate.
moments.takeaway: Li-ion finally wins the recognition it deserves.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Li-ion batteries power phones, laptops, and an exploding electric-vehicle market. Production is ~3 TWh/year (2025). Solid-state batteries are emerging.
now.open_questions: Can solid-state Li batteries become commercial? What replaces cobalt and nickel?

reflection: Goodenough won a Nobel at 97, after decades of being overlooked. Why does recognition come so late to some, so easily to others?
